Thirty million people. That's the most common estimate of how many people in China starved to death between nineteen fifty-nine and nineteen sixty-one. The worst famine anybody has ever counted.
And one year before it started, Mao Zedong's government sent whole cities out to kill a bird. The sparrow.

In the spring of nineteen fifty-eight, about three million people in Peking walked out of their houses at five in the morning. Soldiers, clerks, students, little kids. Banging pots and pans so the sparrows could never land.
The birds flew until they were exhausted. Then they fell out of the sky.
Soon the sparrows were nearly gone. And the bugs they used to eat were not.
And when the hunger came, it didn't come for the men who wrote the plan. It came for the farmers who grew the food, and for their children.
So who decided it? Who stood up and said, stop, this is a mistake? And who paid for it?
Today I'll show you the whole thing. What they were told, who said stop, what happened year by year, and who is still paying.

My name's Ruth Dalby. I grew up on a farm in Kansas, and I've spent my life reading what governments tell farmers to do, and then reading what it cost. That's my kitchen table, with a jar on it, and a dead beetle in the jar. That will make sense in a little while.
This is file number four. Every story here is true. The sources are in the description.

First, the part the funny internet version always leaves out. The sparrows did not cause that famine all by themselves. The people in charge did. The sparrows were just the first warning that nobody in that country was allowed to say stop.
So let's start with the people who made the plan. They weren't cartoon villains. They had a real problem.
China in nineteen fifty-eight was poor. Very poor. Most people were farmers, working small fields by hand.

And disease was everywhere. Flies on the food, mosquitoes in the rice paddies, rats in the grain. When the Communists took over, more than ten million people carried one parasite from the water alone.
The man at the top was Mao Zedong, the chairman of the Communist Party, which had taken power in nineteen forty-nine, nine years before.
And his government did something that, on paper, sounds reasonable. It started a national health campaign. Clean up the country. Kill the pests that make people sick.
They picked four. Rats, flies, mosquitoes, and sparrows. They called it the Four Pests campaign, and it was officially launched in February of nineteen fifty-eight.
Now, three of those four spread disease. The fourth one was on the list for a different reason. Sparrows eat grain.
Each sparrow, they said, eats about four pounds of grain a year. So every sparrow you kill saves four pounds of grain for the people.
I've done that kind of math at my own table. It's tidy, it fits on one line, and it leaves out everything that matters.

That same year, the government launched something much bigger. The Great Leap Forward. The idea was to jump China from a poor farm country to an industrial power in a few years. Catch up with the West, fast.

Farmers were organized into giant communes. Sharing the land, eating together in big common dining halls. And the whole country was told to make steel. In little homemade furnaces, in their backyards.
So picture it. Your village is supposed to grow more grain than ever, kill every sparrow in sight, and make steel in the backyard. With the same pair of hands.
Somebody did warn them about the sparrows. His name was Tso-hsin Cheng.

Cheng was one of China's top bird scientists. An ornithologist, which is just a fancy word for a person who studies birds. He was born in nineteen oh six, and he'd spent his whole career out in the field with them.

And he knew something the officials didn't want to hear. He and his colleagues looked at what tree sparrows actually eat. Yes, they eat some grain. But in the breeding season, when they're feeding their babies, they mostly eat insects.
That's the beetle in my jar. That's what a sparrow is really hunting. In other words, the sparrow was the farmer's pest control, and it never sent a bill. And the government was about to fire it.
Cheng was against the sparrow campaign from the very start. For years, nobody listened.
And here's a detail. When the big day came, the government newspaper reported that more than two thousand staff from the Chinese Academy of Sciences took part in the battle against the sparrows.
The scientists were out there too. Banging pots. That's one way to settle a scientific argument.
Now, the battle itself. That's the word they used, a battle.

Peking, spring of nineteen fifty-eight. At five in the morning, bugles, cymbals and whistles went off across the city. About three million people came out. That's more people than live in all of Chicago today.
Soldiers, students, office workers, schoolchildren. They banged pots and pans, washbasins, anything from the kitchen that made noise. They climbed onto rooftops and waved poles and red flags.
A sparrow can't stay in the air very long. It needs to land and rest.
So if every roof, every tree, every courtyard is full of people screaming and banging, the bird keeps flying. Until it can't.
Then they dropped. Right out of the sky. Exhausted, dead.
What didn't drop, they caught, with nets, with scatter-guns, with long bamboo poles tipped with glue. They smashed the nests, broke the eggs, and killed the chicks.
The government paper in Peking cheered them on. No warrior, it said, shall be withdrawn until the battle is won.
By the count reported in America at the time, about three hundred ten thousand sparrows died in Peking alone. Another four million across the rest of China. And that was just the start.

Children were right in the middle of it. Every child from about five years old up was part of the campaign. Schoolkids were sent out into the countryside at a set hour to hunt. They carried slingshots, and they kept count.

One sixteen-year-old boy from Yunnan, down in the southwest, was held up as a hero. A youth magazine said he'd killed twenty thousand sparrows by himself. He found their trees in the daytime, and came back for them at night.
Years later, a man who'd been a schoolboy in Sichuan back then said it simply. It was fun, wiping out the Four Pests.
And I believe him. Of course it was fun. You're ten years old, and the government hands you a slingshot and calls you a hero. Kids aren't the ones I'm angry at.
Even the foreigners got pulled in. Sparrows started hiding at the Polish embassy, the one place the crowds couldn't go.

As a Polish newspaper later told it, the embassy refused to let them in. So the crowds surrounded it and beat drums. For two days. When it was over, the embassy staff were clearing dead sparrows off the grounds with shovels.

So how many birds died in the end? Nobody really counted. Officials reported numbers like one billion sparrows, and other claims went up to nearly two billion. Careful writers today just say hundreds of millions.
By the early nineteen sixties, the tree sparrow was close to gone in China.
Let's add it up so far. A poor country with real problems. A plan that fit on one line. A scientist who said these birds eat bugs, and three million people banging pots anyway.
Now here's where it goes from foolish to deadly. Year by year.
Nineteen fifty-eight. The sparrows are falling, and so is the truth. Local officials are under pressure to report record harvests.
So they do. Provinces report record grain hauls, and the figures are fake.

At the same time, farmers are told to plant their seeds much closer together and plow much deeper. That came partly from the ideas of a Soviet scientist named Trofim Lysenko, who promised plants wouldn't compete for space. Any farmer could have told him different. The plants crowded each other out, and the yields went down.
And a lot of the men who should have been bringing in that harvest were out feeding the backyard steel furnaces instead.
On paper, China had never grown so much grain. The trouble is, you can't eat paper.
Nineteen fifty-nine. This is the year it turns.

On March twenty-fifth, nineteen fifty-nine, at a secret meeting in Shanghai, Mao Zedong told the party to collect up to one third of all the available grain. Much more than the state had ever taken before.
And the notes from that meeting record him saying this. When there is not enough to eat, people starve to death. It is better to let half of the people die, so that the other half can eat their fill.
I've read that sentence a lot of times. It doesn't get any easier.

Here's the part that surprised me. Economists went back and studied the numbers from that year. In nineteen fifty-nine, when the famine began, China grew almost three times the food its people needed to survive.
Three times. And people were starving anyway.
Even stranger, the places that grew the most food per person that year had more deaths, not fewer. Because the government was counting on those places, and it took the grain out.
So the famine wasn't just a shortage. It was a collection system that couldn't hear bad news.

And that summer, somebody did try to give it some bad news. In July of nineteen fifty-nine, at a party meeting in the mountains at Lushan, the defense minister, Peng Dehuai, wrote Mao a private letter. He said the harvest reports were exaggerated. He criticized the backyard furnaces.
Mao made the letter public and turned it against him. By September, Peng was out as defense minister. Later he was persecuted, and he died in nineteen seventy-four.
In that system, the reward for telling the truth was losing everything. So after Lushan, the truth got very quiet.

There was one small win that year. Cheng, the bird scientist, finally got heard. In nineteen fifty-nine, he helped push a decision against killing more sparrows. It would take months for it to become official.
Nineteen sixty. The worst year.
Without the sparrows, insects that eat the crops had fewer enemies. Locusts and other bugs boomed. In nineteen sixty, locusts swarmed out of control, in the same year as a terrible drought.
And on March eighteenth, nineteen sixty, Mao gave a new order. Stop killing sparrows. Replace them with bedbugs.
A few weeks later, on April tenth, the official list was rewritten. Rats, bedbugs, flies and mosquitoes.
I'll give them this much. Bedbugs don't eat locusts.
But taking a bird off a list doesn't bring it back. And by then, the hunger was everywhere.

In Xinyang, in Henan province, the very center of the famine, people wrote letters begging for help. The post office took more than a thousand of those letters and never delivered them. People who tried to leave to find food were sent to labor camps.
And all through it, there was still grain in the government warehouses. At the worst time, China was still exporting grain to other countries.
Grain output fell by more than a quarter in nineteen sixty and sixty-one.
Nineteen sixty-one. The deaths keep piling up. The leaders finally start to back off, and China begins buying grain from abroad.
There was a young man named Yang Jisheng, eighteen years old, away at boarding school. The uncle who had raised him, the man he called father, was starving. Yang rushed home. He got there too late.
For years, Yang blamed himself. He thought, if I had stayed home and helped him dig up his crops, he'd still be alive. He didn't know the same thing was happening in millions of homes.
Much later, as a journalist, Yang spent ten years digging through government archives. His count is thirty-six million dead. His book is called Tombstone, and it is banned in China to this day.
By nineteen sixty-two, the famine was over.
So now, the number in the title. Thirty million. Here's where it comes from.

Demographers, people who study births and deaths, rebuilt the population numbers year by year. The best of those studies land at about thirty million deaths. Estimates run from around fifteen million on the low side, to forty-five million or more on the high side.
Thirty million is close to the whole population of Texas today. Gone in three years.
And about the same number of babies were never born, or were born years later than they would have been.
Now, I promised to be honest with you about the sparrows. So here it is.

In twenty twenty-five, a team of economists put the old harvest records next to maps of where sparrows used to live. In the places where sparrows had been common, rice and wheat harvests fell harder after the birds were killed. They estimate the sparrow campaign alone led to nearly two million extra deaths.
Two million. That's about one death in fifteen. A terrible number.
And it means the other fourteen came from the rest of the plan. The fake reports, the grain they took, the steel furnaces. And the man who couldn't be told no.

The sparrows didn't starve China. But they tell you exactly how China got starved. Somebody in an office decided he knew better than nature, and better than the farmers. And everybody who said otherwise got shouted down.
So who's still paying?
Start with the babies. In the Wuhu region of Anhui province, one of the hardest-hit places, the birth rate fell by about eighty percent from nineteen fifty-nine to nineteen sixty.

And the children who were carried through that hunger in their mothers' bellies grew up with a higher risk of schizophrenia. A study in a major American medical journal found the risk was more than double for babies born there in nineteen sixty.
The babies born in nineteen sixty are sixty-six years old this year. My age. And they're still carrying it.
Then there's the man who was right.

During the Cultural Revolution, in the late sixties, Cheng was punished for opposing the sparrow campaign. He was told that birds are public animals of capitalism. He had to wear a badge that said reactionary. They cut his pay to almost nothing.
They kept him alone in a cowshed for six months. They made him sweep the halls and clean the toilets.
The man who was wrong blamed the weather. The man who was right got the toilets.

And the official history still leans that way. Chinese official histories partly blame the famine on bad weather and on the Soviet experts going home. Yang Jisheng says those excuses don't hold water. I'm with Yang.
Now, what actually worked? Because something did.

First, the sparrows came back. Slowly, on their own, the way nature does when you quit fighting it. Today the tree sparrow numbers in the hundreds of millions again. Scientists list it as a species of least concern.
Second, Cheng kept working. He lived to be ninety-one, and he spent the rest of his life studying China's birds. The science was right the whole time. It just needed somebody in power to listen.
And third, the farmers fixed what the men in the offices broke.

In nineteen seventy-eight, in a little village called Xiaogang, in Anhui province, the same province that had starved twenty years before, eighteen farmers crept into a mud hut one evening. They were hungry. They'd been begging for food in other villages.
They signed a secret contract. Each family would farm its own piece of land, give the government its share, and keep the rest.
And they wrote this. If we are put in prison or executed, we will not complain. And the others in the group will raise our children to eighteen years old.
They hid that paper inside a piece of bamboo in the roof.
That first season, they grew more food than they had in the previous five years put together. Same land, same tools, same farmers. The only thing that changed was who got to decide.
Within a few years, farms all over China had picked up the same idea.
So here's what I take from it, sitting at this kitchen table.
The sparrow was never the pest. The pest was a plan that nobody was allowed to argue with.

Every farmer I've ever known has a little bit of Cheng in them. You watch the field, you see what eats what. You learn that the bird you curse in the spring is the reason you've got a crop in the fall.
The trouble starts when somebody far away, who has never stood in your field, decides he knows it better than you do. And then makes it a crime to disagree.
That's the lesson, and it's the same one every time. When the people who do the work aren't allowed to say stop, the bill always comes to the people who do the work.

Now I want to hear from you. Has somebody in an office ever told your family to kill something, or plow something, or spray something, that turned out to be helping all along? Tell me what it was in the comments. I read every one.
If you want the next file when it comes out, subscribe and turn on the bell. A new file every week.
Next time, we're going to the other side of the world, to a sea that disappeared. The file is called, Fishermen Woke Up and the Sea Was Gone. Who Took It.
I'm Ruth Dalby. Leave the sparrows alone.
